The first word is a door that opens onto nothing in particular, just air and the slight smell of paper that has been sitting in a drawer too long. I have a thousand words and I do not know where they want to go, which is perhaps the only honest starting point. I think of rain on a roof that is not mine, the way it makes a rhythm that sounds like someone tapping a message in Morse code but without the urgency of a message, just the persistence of weather doing its eternal work. The cup on my desk is blue, a blue so deep it could be a hole in the sky, and I have been staring at it for longer than is healthy, wondering if objects have memories of the hands that held them. Probably not, but the thought is pleasant, like a small lie that doesn’t hurt anyone.

There was a library once, in a city I have almost forgotten the name of, where the stairs creaked in a specific key, a kind of D-sharp complaint, and the librarian had a mustache that seemed to predate modern electricity. I spent an afternoon there reading the footnotes in a book about maritime law from 1847, convinced that the real story was always hidden in the margins, that history was a secret kept by people who didn’t know they were keeping it. The dust smelled like cinnamon and old glue. I remember the light came through windows that were too high to see out of but just low enough to let in a golden rectangle that moved across the floor like a slow animal. I want to go back, but maybe that library only exists now inside this sentence, which is also fine. We build museums out of sentences. We archive the past by describing it badly.

Time is not a line but a puddle. You drop something into it and the ripples overlap with ripples you made yesterday, or last year, or in a dream where you were someone else entirely. I have been thinking about repetition lately: how every morning the coffee machine makes the same sound of betrayal—the hiss, the grumble, the final drip like a clock running down. We call it routine and pretend it doesn’t contain a small death, the death of possibility, but I think possibility is more resilient than that. It just waits under the surface. It is the thing that makes you look up from your phone at the exact moment a bird lands on the fence, and for a second you are not yourself but the noticing of the bird, which is a kind of transcendence cheap enough for anyone to afford.

The train station at three in the morning is not a place but a feeling. The lights are too bright for the hour, fluorescent stars that refuse to flicker out. There is a vending machine that only sells crackers that taste like cardboard and regret, and a bench where someone has left a newspaper with a headline that says “Everything Changes,” which is technically true and philosophically useless. I am waiting for a train that may not come, or that may come and take me to a city where I have never been but somehow recognize the buildings because they are built from my expectations. This is how travel works: we arrive already edited by anticipation.

Back to the screen. The cursor blinks. It is a heart that has forgotten how to beat continuously, a mechanical insistence. I am writing because writing is the only way I know to think without stopping, and even then I stop, I pause, I look out the window where nothing special is happening and that is the point. Nothing special is the background against which everything else tries to shine. The trees are just being trees, the cars are just being cars, and I am just being a creature who types words into a void that might or might not be listening. But the void listens differently. It absorbs, it reflects, it sometimes answers in the form of a reply hours later, a like, a share, a silence that feels like agreement.

I make a list of small observations, because lists are honest; they don’t pretend to be poetry:
The way light falls on a kitchen counter when the sun is at forty-five degrees and the window is dirty.
The sound of a door closing softly, as if the door is sorry for being loud.
How a name you haven’t thought of in years can appear suddenly in your mouth like a taste, sweet or sour.
The particular disappointment of a cloud that looks like it might rain and then decides not to.
The way cats sit in windows as if they are the kings of a kingdom that only they can see.

These things do not need analysis. They need only to be noted, like weather in a journal that will eventually be lost, which is okay because the act of noting is the true archive.

I think sometimes about the word “whatever.” It is a shrug made of letters, a refusal to choose, and yet it is the most democratic word in English. It allows everything to be included: whatever happens, whatever you want, whatever remains. I have used it as a title, a defense, a spell. “Write whatever comes to you.” And so here I am, writing whatever, which turns out to be this: a collection of fragments that do not resolve but accumulate, like snow against a door that will eventually hold it back or give in, depending on the weather, depending on the door, depending on the patience of the snow.

The sound of a refrigerator is a kind of white noise that becomes audible only when everything else stops. I have been listening to it for years, this electric hum that says “life is continuing,” and I think of it as the baseline of modern existence, the drone that allows other sounds to exist in contrast. Without it, the silence would be too loud, too demanding. We need our background hums; they are the canvas on which we paint our attention.

I once met someone who said they could taste colors. Not as a metaphor—they actually perceived flavors when they looked at paintings. I was jealous and skeptical in equal measure. I asked them what blue tasted like and they said “salt and the bottom of the ocean.” I have never forgotten that. It seems to me that all perception is translation, that we are constantly turning one language into another, light into thought, sound into emotion, feeling into word. The cup is blue, but it is also a feeling of calm, and that feeling is also a memory of a room with windows, and that room is also this sentence, and this sentence is also you, reading, converting my words into your version of these thoughts.

The concept of “now” is slippery. You try to capture it and it has already become “then.” The best we can do is approximate, to write in the present tense as if we are living inside the moment, which is a kind of fiction we all agree to. I am writing this now, in the now that is already passing, and by the time you read these lines they will be then, and I will be then or I will be gone, and the blue cup will have been washed or broken or moved to another desk, and the rain will have fallen on other roofs, and the library will still exist only in the sentence, which is also then, which is also now, which is also never quite either.

I think about death briefly, as one does when the day is long and the words are running out. Not death as drama, but death as the ultimate punctuation, the period at the end of a book that is too long to read and too short to matter. It is not a failure, just a boundary. And boundaries are what give shape to everything else. Without death, life is not a narrative; it is an infinite loop, a humming refrigerator with no off switch. The limitation is the gift. The thousand words are a gift because they end.

So let me end. The cup remains. The words remain, but only as long as they are read, and even then they change. Write whatever comes to you. It came to me. It was this. It is enough. The rain is still falling where it needs to fall. The cursor blinks. The door is open.
